modules.comments:
Pure Force Engine

A clean, debuggable force simulation engine. The forces are PureScript
(`hylograph-forces`: d3-force's, bit for bit, and more); the loop is
this library's own. There is no D3 in it.

What that buys over d3.forceSimulation:
- Full control over when forces run
- Predictable, debuggable behavior
- Clean PureScript types
- No hidden state or timers

Usage:
```purescript
import Hylograph.ForceEngine as FE

main = do
  sim <- FE.create FE.defaultConfig
  FE.setNodes myNodes sim
  FE.addForce (FE.ManyBody "charge" FE.defaultManyBody) sim
  FE.onTick (renderNodes sim) sim
  FE.start sim
```

Events that can occur during simulation lifecycle.

These types are primarily for Halogen integration via subscriptions.
Internally, callbacks are invoked directly without constructing these values.

Usage with Halogen:
```purescript
handleAction (SimEvent event) = case event of
  Tick -> liftEffect updateDOMPositions
  Started -> H.modify_ _ { simRunning = true }
  Stopped -> H.modify_ _ { simRunning = false }
  AlphaDecayed alpha -> when (alpha < 0.1) $ liftEffect doSomething
```

declarations.comments:
Callbacks for simulation events.

All callbacks are stored in Refs to allow dynamic updates and to keep
the tick loop allocation-free (no closures created per-tick).

The callbacks are `Effect Unit` rather than taking event data because:
1. Performance: No boxing/unboxing of event data in hot path
2. Simplicity: Consumers can read simulation state directly if needed
3. Flexibility: The consumer decides what data they need
declarations.title: SimulationCallbacks

Keep it fast! Avoid allocations, complex logic, or console.log.

```purescript

```

Bad:
```purescript
onSimulationTick (do
  nodes <- Ref.read nodesRef  -- Extra ref read
  log "tick"                   -- Console I/O
  H.tell ...                   -- Halogen message (allocates)
) callbacks
```

declarations.comments:
Swizzle links by looking up nodes by their index field

USE THIS when working with a FILTERED node subset where array positions
don't match node.index values. Looks up nodes by their `.index` field
and silently drops links where either endpoint is not found.

PERFORMANCE: Uses FFI-backed IntMap for O(1) lookups instead of O(n) find.

This is essential for GUP patterns where you show only a subset of nodes.

Example:
```purescript
let visibleNodes = filter isVisible allNodes
    swizzled = swizzleLinksByIndex _.index visibleNodes links \src tgt i link ->
      { source: src, target: tgt, index: i, value: link.value }
```
declarations.title: swizzleLinksByIndex

declarations.comments:
Convert raw links (integer indices) to swizzled links (node references)

Expects `link.source` and `link.target` to be valid *array indices* into the
`nodes` array. Links with out-of-bounds indices are silently dropped.

Note: If your link indices are *semantic* (node.index field values) rather than
array positions, use `swizzleLinksByIndex` instead, which looks up nodes by
their `.index` field.

The transform function allows you to build the output link record,
copying extra fields from the raw link as needed.

Example:
```purescript
let swizzled = swizzleLinks nodes rawLinks \src tgt i link ->
      { source: src, target: tgt, index: i, value: link.value }
```
declarations.title: swizzleLinks

declarations.comments:
Filter links to only those where both endpoints are in the node subset

PERFORMANCE: Uses FFI-backed IntSet for O(1) membership instead of O(n) elem.

Use this before swizzling when you want to show links only between
visible/selected nodes. Pairs naturally with `swizzleLinksByIndex`.

Example:
```purescript
let visibleNodes = filter isVisible allNodes
    visibleLinks = filterLinksToSubset _.index visibleNodes allLinks
    swizzled = swizzleLinksByIndex _.index visibleNodes visibleLinks transform
```
declarations.title: filterLinksToSubset

modules.comments:
Force Engine Core

The simulation loop's parts: forces, the position update, cooling, the
animation frame and dragging.

The forces are `hylograph-forces`: d3-force's seven and the Rust
kernel's additions, in PureScript, with no D3 anywhere. A force is made in
two steps, because a simulation is usually described before its nodes
exist:

1. a `ForceRecipe` says what the force is (`createManyBody config`, or
   `Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup.recipe` for anything a `Setup` can say);
2. `initializeForce` gives it the nodes and links and returns a
   `ForceHandle`, which `applyForce` applies each tick.

Per-node and per-link values are read when the force is initialized, so
a force has to be initialized again (`reinitializeForce`) when the nodes,
the links, or anything those values are computed from have changed.

Coincident nodes are separated by a seeded generator (`RandomSource`),
one per simulation, so the same nodes, links and forces give the same
layout every time.

1. Callbacks are `Effect Unit` - no monadic overhead in hot path

3. Event types are for documentation/Halogen integration, not for internal use

modules.comments:
Link Operations for Force Simulations

Functions for working with links in force-directed graphs:
- Swizzling: converting index-based links to node-reference links
- Filtering: selecting links for node subsets

These operations are essential for:
- Rendering (need node references to read x,y positions)
- GUP patterns (filtering to visible nodes)
- Dynamic graph updates

PERFORMANCE: Hot-path functions use FFI-backed O(1) Set/Map lookups
instead of O(n) array scans to handle 1000+ node graphs at 60fps.

declarations.comments:
Convert raw links (integer indices) to swizzled links (node references)

Expects `link.source` and `link.target` to be valid *array indices* into the
`nodes` array. Links with out-of-bounds indices are silently dropped.

Note: If your link indices are *semantic* (node.index field values) rather than
array positions, use `swizzleLinksByIndex` instead, which looks up nodes by
their `.index` field.

The transform function allows you to build the output link record,
copying extra fields from the raw link as needed.

Example:
```purescript
let swizzled = swizzleLinks nodes rawLinks \src tgt i link ->
      { source: src, target: tgt, index: i, value: link.value }
```
declarations.title: swizzleLinks

declarations.comments:
Swizzle links by looking up nodes by their index field

USE THIS when working with a FILTERED node subset where array positions
don't match node.index values. Looks up nodes by their `.index` field
and silently drops links where either endpoint is not found.

PERFORMANCE: Uses FFI-backed IntMap for O(1) lookups instead of O(n) find.

This is essential for GUP patterns where you show only a subset of nodes.

Example:
```purescript
let visibleNodes = filter isVisible allNodes
    swizzled = swizzleLinksByIndex _.index visibleNodes links \src tgt i link ->
      { source: src, target: tgt, index: i, value: link.value }
```
declarations.title: swizzleLinksByIndex

declarations.comments:
Filter links to only those where both endpoints are in the node subset

PERFORMANCE: Uses FFI-backed IntSet for O(1) membership instead of O(n) elem.

Use this before swizzling when you want to show links only between
visible/selected nodes. Pairs naturally with `swizzleLinksByIndex`.

Example:
```purescript
let visibleNodes = filter isVisible allNodes
    visibleLinks = filterLinksToSubset _.index visibleNodes allLinks
    swizzled = swizzleLinksByIndex _.index visibleNodes visibleLinks transform
```
declarations.title: filterLinksToSubset

modules.comments:
Force Simulation Rendering

FFI-optimized helpers for rendering force-directed graphs.

IMPORTANT PATTERN: For simulations, bind data ONCE then update positions via FFI.
Do NOT use Tree API or data joins in tick callbacks - they are O(n) per tick.

Correct usage:
```purescript
-- Define group IDs (type-safe, no typos)
nodesGroup = GroupId "#my-nodes"
linksGroup = GroupId "#my-links"

-- At initialization (once):
nodeSel <- appendData Circle nodes [cx _.x, cy _.y, ...]
linkSel <- appendData Line swizzledLinks [x1 (\l -> l.source.x), ...]

-- In tick callback (every frame):
updateCirclePositions nodesGroup
updateLinkPositions linksGroup
```

The FFI updates set attributes straight from each element's bound datum:
O(n) DOM updates with no data join, and no D3.

declarations.comments:
A type-safe wrapper for DOM selector strings.

Use this to identify groups of elements for position updates.
The newtype provides compile-time checking that you're using
group IDs consistently, without any runtime overhead.

Example:
```purescript
-- Define once, use everywhere
packageNodes :: GroupId
packageNodes = GroupId "#package-nodes"

moduleNodes :: GroupId
moduleNodes = GroupId "#module-nodes"
```
declarations.title: GroupId

declarations.comments:
Update circle positions (cx, cy) from bound data's x, y fields.

Assumes data bound to circles has `x :: Number` and `y :: Number` fields.
Uses D3's `selection.attr()` which reads from `__data__` on each element.

Example:
```purescript
nodesGroup :: GroupId
nodesGroup = GroupId "#nodes"

updateCirclePositions nodesGroup
```
declarations.title: updateCirclePositions

declarations.comments:
Update line positions (x1, y1, x2, y2) from bound data's source/target nodes.

Assumes data bound to lines has:
- `source :: { x :: Number, y :: Number, ... }`
- `target :: { x :: Number, y :: Number, ... }`

This is the "swizzled link" format where source/target are node objects,
not integer indices. Use `Sim.getSwizzledLinks` after adding a Link force.

Example:
```purescript
linksGroup :: GroupId
linksGroup = GroupId "#links"

updateLinkPositions linksGroup
```
declarations.title: updateLinkPositions

declarations.comments:
Update group positions (transform) from bound data's x, y fields.

Selects `g.module-pack` elements and updates their transform attribute.
Assumes data bound to groups has `x :: Number` and `y :: Number` fields.

Example:
```purescript
nodesGroup :: GroupId
nodesGroup = GroupId "#nodes"

updateGroupPositions nodesGroup
```
declarations.title: updateGroupPositions

declarations.comments:
Update tree link paths (d attribute) from bound data's source/target nodes.

Expects data bound to path elements has:
- `source :: Int` (node ID)
- `target :: Int` (node ID)

This function looks up node positions from the DOM (circles) and computes
vertical bezier paths. Used for animating tree links during transitions.

Example:
```purescript
linksGroup :: GroupId
linksGroup = GroupId "#explorer-links"

updateTreeLinkPaths linksGroup
```

element under the group; each element's bound datum is its `__data__`.
(Until 2026-11-18 the setter was handed a D3 selection.)

modules.name: Hylograph.ForceEngine.Render

modules.comments:
Declarative Force Setup

Unified system for declaratively configuring force simulations.
Replaces the older ForceSpec (too simple) and Config.* modules (wrong abstraction layer).

Key features:
- Static or dynamic (per-node, or per-link) parameter values
- Optional filters to apply forces selectively
- Idempotent `applySetup` that works for both initial setup and updates

Example:
```purescript
mySetup = setup "physics"
  [ manyBody "charge" # withStrength (static (-30.0))
  , collide "collision" # withRadius (dynamic _.r)
  , positionX "gridX" # withX (dynamic _.gridX) # withStrength (static 0.1)
  , positionY "gridY" # withY (dynamic _.gridY) # withStrength (static 0.1)
  ]

-- Apply to simulation (idempotent - can call repeatedly)
applySetup mySetup sim

-- Update: just call applySetup with new config
applySetup (mySetup # removeForce "charge") sim
```

A force is one constructor of `ForceConfig`, carrying a record of exactly
the parameters that force has. The smart constructors (`manyBody`,
`collide`, ...) and the `with...` builders are the intended way to make
one; a builder that does not apply to a force leaves it unchanged.

Seven forces are d3-force's. Five are not (`towards`, `rectCollide`,
`contain`, `cohesion`, `directional`), nor is a many-body force scoped
by group, nor a collision with a filter or scaled by alpha. Both engines
run all of them: `applySetup` here is the default engine
(`hylograph-forces`, PureScript, no D3), and
`Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup.WASM.applySetup` is the Rust/WASM kernel.

Which pairs of nodes a many-body force acts between. A node whose group
is `Nothing` is in no group: it has no same-group pairs, and is in a
different group from everyone.

declarations.comments:
Circles that must not overlap.

A node the filter leaves out collides with nothing. With `alphaScaled` the strength used is
strength * alpha, so the collision weakens as the simulation cools and
gives way to forces that hold a node at a place; without it (d3's
collide) a collision is as hard at rest as in flight.

declarations.title: LinkConfig

declarations.comments: Move the mean position of all nodes toward a point.

declarations.title: PositionConfig

declarations.comments: Pull toward a circle of a given radius around (x, y).
declarations.title: RadialConfig

declarations.comments:
A spring from each node to its own target point:
v += (target - position) * strength * alpha. `Nothing` leaves a node
alone. For morphing between layouts: on the WASM engine the targets can
be replaced between ticks without re-applying the setup
(`Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup.WASM.retarget`); on the default engine,
apply the setup again.
declarations.title: TowardsConfig

declarations.comments:
Axis-aligned rectangles (for labels) that must not
overlap: an overlapping pair is pushed apart along the axis on which it
overlaps least, the larger rectangle moving less. A pinned rectangle
(`fx`, `fy`) is never moved, and what overlaps it takes the whole push.

A node the filter leaves out collides with nothing. `scope` restricts
the pairs by group: only two nodes of the same group, or only two nodes
not of the same group (labels against dots, say, and not each other).

`throughSqueeze`: a rectangle pushed from both sides on an axis goes
through one of them instead of staying where the pushes cancel (the way
it is already moving, else with the stronger side). That is what
resolves crowded wide rectangles, and it wants nothing else pressing
them together: under a pull that does not die away, a rectangle is
walked through its neighbour. The rule in full is on
`Hylograph.Forces.RectCollide`.
declarations.title: RectCollideConfig

declarations.comments:
Keep nodes inside regions. Each node is confined to
`regions !! i` where `region node == Just i` (`Nothing`: free). What is
kept inside is the node's body: a rectangle of `halfWidth` by
`halfHeight` grown all round by `radius` (a circle when the half-extents
are 0, as they are by default; in a circular region a rectangle counts
as the circle round it). `strength` (0 to 1) steers a node that is
about to leave back toward the nearest allowed point; `hard` also clamps
positions into the region after each tick, so that no node is ever
drawn outside.
declarations.title: ContainConfig

declarations.comments: A region nodes can be confined to.
declarations.title: Region

declarations.comments:
Pull each node toward the centroid of its group:
v += (centroid - position) * strength * alpha. `Nothing`: in no group.
declarations.title: CohesionConfig

declarations.comments:
Over the simulation's links: push each link's target
to be at least `gap` beyond its source along `axis` (children below
parents, with axis (0, 1)). Links already that far apart are left alone.

As a force it is scaled by alpha and shared with everything else that
pushes, so the gap it leaves can be well short of the one asked for.
With `hard` the links are also projected after each tick, so that the
gap asked for is the gap kept: a link short of its gap moves its target
along the axis by the shortfall (its source back, if the target is
pinned and the source is not).

This is idempotent - calling with the same setup does minimal work:
- Forces in setup but not simulation: create and add
- Forces in simulation but not setup: remove

Every force is made afresh for the simulation's current nodes and links:
`dynamic` values, filters, groups and regions are evaluated then, once
per node or per link. Apply the setup again after changing what they
read. Each tick applies the forces in order of their names.

Throws, before changing anything, if a link names a node that is not
among the nodes and the setup has a force along the links (`node not
found: <id>`, as d3-force says it). `tryApplySetup` returns that as a
value instead.

The setup's params (alpha, alphaMin, alphaDecay, alphaTarget,
velocityRetention) become the simulation's, replacing what it was
created with.

Example:
```purescript
-- Initial setup
applySetup mySetup sim

-- Later: update setup (just call again)
applySetup (mySetup # removeForce "charge") sim
```

This function handles three concerns:
1. Force configuration (same as applySetup)
2. Node GUP: diff desired nodes vs current, merge simulation state for updates
3. Link GUP: diff desired links vs current

Simulation state preservation (for updated nodes):
- x, y: Current position (preserved)
- vx, vy: Current velocity (preserved)
- fx, fy: Pinned position (preserved)
- All other fields: Taken from desired nodes

Example usage:
```purescript
-- Stop simulation before transition
Sim.stop sim

-- Apply new configuration and data
result <- applySetupWithData mySetup newNodes newLinks sim

-- Use result for animations
animateEnter result.nodes.entered
animateExit result.nodes.exited

-- Restart simulation
Sim.reheat sim
```

modules.comments:
WASM Force Setup

Declarative force configuration for WASM simulation engine.
Uses the same Setup types as the default engine, and means the same.

What a `Setup` means here, force by force, is what it means to the
default engine (`Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup.applySetup`), and
`test/engine-parity.mjs` holds the two to each other:
- any number of forces of any type; a later force replaces an earlier
  one of the same name, and each tick applies them in name order (the
  default engine keeps them in a `Map` keyed by name);
- links name their endpoints by node `id`, not by array position;
- new nodes are initialized as d3 initializes them
  (`Hylograph.ForceEngine.Core.initializeNodes`).

`Dynamic` values, filters, groups and regions are evaluated once per
node (or per link) when the setup is applied and handed to the kernel
as arrays; the kernel never calls back into JavaScript.

Both engines are deterministic: the same nodes, links and setup give the
same positions on every run. The kernel computes in f32 and the default
engine in f64, so the two agree to float width over one tick and drift
apart after that, as any two roundings of a force layout do.

The nodes a caller is handed (`getNodes`, `step`) are fresh records
after every tick, not the same objects moved, which is the one way this
engine differs from the default one. A pin set on the latest ones
(`node.fx`, as a drag does) is read before the next tick.

Example:
```purescript
import Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup (setup, manyBody, center, withStrength, static)
import Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup.WASM as WASM

mySetup = setup "physics"
  [ manyBody "charge" # withStrength (static (-30.0))
  , center "center" # withX (static 0.0) # withY (static 0.0)
  ]

main = do
  WASM.initWasm "./pkg/force_kernel.js"
  sim <- WASM.create initialNodes initialLinks
  result <- WASM.applySetupWithData mySetup newNodes newLinks sim
  -- Use result.nodes.entered, result.nodes.exited for animations
```

3. Link GUP: diff desired vs current

Simulation state preserved for updated nodes:

- vx, vy: Current velocity
- fx, fy: Pinned position

Example:

as the layout settles.
declarations.title: kineticEnergy

declarations.comments: The furthest any node moved during the last tick.
declarations.title: maxDisplacement

declarations.comments:
The largest change in any node's step between the last two ticks: the
acceleration it actually underwent.

This is what `kineticEnergy` and `maxDisplacement` cannot see. A node on
a spring is momentarily still at the far end of every swing, and nodes
released together swing in step, so both of those vanish there, far from
rest. The acceleration is then at its largest. 0 until two ticks have
been made since the simulation was created, restored or resized.
declarations.title: maxAcceleration

declarations.comments:
Is the simulation at rest? True when, over the last two ticks, no node
moved further than `step` in a tick and no node's step changed by more
than `acceleration`. False until two ticks have been made.

It is measured from positions, so it is right whatever moved a node, and
a node held against a hard region by a force that keeps pushing counts
as at rest. It says what the last two ticks did: after `retarget`, tick
before asking.

For a node on a spring of stiffness k (a `towards` of that strength, at
alpha 1) with velocity retention r, the node is then within
(acceleration + (1 - r) * (step + acceleration)) / (k * r) of where it
will stop, and gets no further away. Stop on the first tick it is true.
declarations.title: settled

modules.comments:
Force Engine Simulation

High-level API for running force simulations.
This module provides a clean interface for:
- Creating and configuring simulations
- Running the animation loop
- Handling tick callbacks for rendering

The forces are PureScript (`hylograph-forces`: d3-force's seven,
bit for bit, and the Rust kernel's additions). There is no D3 here. Each
simulation has its own seeded generator for separating coincident nodes,
so the same nodes, links and forces give the same layout every time.

== IMPORTANT: forces read their values when they are initialized

A force evaluates its per-node and per-link values (targets, radii,
strengths, filters) once, when it is given its nodes. If you update
`node.gridX` and call `reheat`, a force whose target reads `gridX` still
has the old values. `setNodes`, `setLinks`, `reinitializeForces` and
`updateGridXYAndReinit` make every force again from its recipe.

`node.gridX` alone changes nothing.

Attach simulation-aware drag behavior to node elements

1. Reheat the simulation on drag start
2. Update fx/fy (fixed position) during drag

- Subsequent drags: if you barely move (< 3px), unpins the node

This is useful for force playgrounds and exploration where users want
to "fix" certain nodes in place while letting others float freely.

Example:

modules.comments:
WASM Force Engine

High-performance force simulation using Rust/WebAssembly.
Faster than the default (PureScript) kernel; the README has the
measurement.

Usage:
```purescript
import Hylograph.ForceEngine.WASM as WASM

main = do
  -- Initialize WASM module (once at app startup)
  WASM.initWasm "./pkg/force_kernel.js"

  -- Create simulation
  sim <- WASM.create 1000

  -- Configure forces
  WASM.configureManyBody sim { strength: -30.0, theta: 0.9, distanceMin: 1.0, distanceMax: 10000.0 }
  WASM.configureLinks sim { distance: 30.0, strength: 1.0, iterations: 1 }
  WASM.configureCenter sim { x: 0.0, y: 0.0, strength: 1.0 }

  -- Set links
  WASM.setLinks sim [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]  -- [source, target, source, target, ...]

  -- Run simulation
  WASM.tick sim

  -- Get results
  positions <- WASM.getPositions sim  -- [x0, y0, x1, y1, ...]
```

modules.comments:
WASM Engine Adapter

High-performance force simulation using Rust/WebAssembly.
Drop-in replacement for the D3.js-based simulation.

Force calculations are offloaded to compiled WebAssembly. Informally
observed to be faster than the D3 kernel on large graphs; no benchmark
is stored and the figure has not been re-measured.

Usage:
```purescript
import Hylograph.ForceEngine.WASMEngine as WASMEngine

main = do
  -- Initialize WASM module (once at app startup)
  WASMEngine.initWasm "./pkg/force_kernel.js"

  -- Create WASM simulation with nodes
  wasmSim <- WASMEngine.create nodes links config

  -- Create adapter for Scene Engine
  let adapter = WASMEngine.mkAdapter wasmSim

  -- Use with Scene Engine
  engine <- Engine.createEngine adapter
```

modules.comments:
Scene Engine

Tick-based scene orchestration with adapter pattern.

The engine manages transitions between scenes using a three-phase lifecycle:
1. Initialize: Apply init rules to prepare starting state
2. Transition: Interpolate positions from start to target
3. Finalize: Apply final rules and enter stable mode

The engine is generic over the node type. Apps provide an adapter
record with functions that interact with their specific simulation.

Example usage:
```purescript
-- Create adapter for your simulation
adapter = mkAdapter mySimulation

-- Create engine
engineRef <- createEngine adapter

-- Transition to a scene
transitionTo treeFormScene engineRef

-- Call tick from your simulation's tick handler
Sim.onTick (\_ -> tick engineRef) mySimulation
```

declarations.comments:
Adapter functions that connect the engine to your simulation.

The engine is generic - it doesn't know about `Sim.Simulation` directly.
Instead, you provide these adapter functions that do the actual work.

Example adapter for ce-website:
```purescript
mkAdapter :: CESimulation -> EngineAdapter (SimulationNode row)
mkAdapter sim =
  { getNodes: Sim.getNodes sim
  , capturePositions: \nodes -> Object.fromFoldable $
      map (\n -> Tuple (show n.id) { x: n.x, y: n.y }) nodes
  , interpolatePositions: \start target progress ->
      Sim.interpolatePositionsInPlace start target progress sim
  , updatePositions: \positions ->
      Sim.updatePositionsInPlace positions sim
  , applyRulesInPlace: \rules ->
      applyRulesInPlace_ rules sim.nodes
  , reinitializeForces: reinitForcesFor sim
  , reheat: Sim.reheat sim
  }
```

declarations.comments:
Scene configuration with three-phase lifecycle.

**Phase 1: Initialize** (`initRules`)
Applied before transition starts. Use this to set up starting positions,
e.g., moving tree nodes to the root for a "grow from root" animation.

**Phase 2: Transition** (`layout`)
The interpolation engine smoothly moves nodes from their current positions
to the target positions computed by the layout function.

**Phase 3: Finalize** (`finalRules`)
Applied after transition completes. Use this to set up the stable state,
e.g., unpinning nodes so forces can take over, or setting gridX/gridY.

Example:
```purescript
treeFormScene :: SceneConfig MyNode
treeFormScene =
  { name: "TreeForm"
  , initRules: [ moveToRootRule ]
  , layout: \nodes -> computeTreePositions nodes
  , finalRules: \_ -> [ pinAtTreePositionsRule ]
  , stableMode: Static
  }
```

modules.comments:
Scene Handle

Opaque handle for scene-based visualizations.
Wraps simulation + scene engine + transition state.
User never sees Refs - just pure-looking Effect operations.

This is the high-level API for sophisticated visualizations with:
- Choreographed scene transitions (Init → Interpolate → Finalize)
- Node filtering (for focus/neighborhood views)
- GUP-style enter/exit animations

Example usage:
```purescript
-- Create handle with callbacks
handle <- Scene.create config callbacks nodes links renderFn

-- Transition to a scene
Scene.transitionTo treeFormScene handle

-- In your animation loop
continuing <- Scene.onTick handle
when continuing $ requestAnimationFrame (const $ ...)

-- Clean up
Scene.destroy handle
```

Common rule builders and transforms for scene orchestration.

Rules are applied with first-match-wins semantics (CSS-like cascade).
Each rule has a selector (predicate) and a transform function.

This module provides:
- Rule builders for creating rules
- Common transforms (pin, unpin, setGridXY)
- Rule application functions

modules.comments:
Hylograph Force Simulation

High-level API for running force-directed simulations.
Two engines with the same interface: the default, in PureScript
(`hylograph-forces`, no D3), and the Rust/WASM kernel.

## Quick Start

```purescript
import Hylograph.Simulation (runSimulation, Engine(..), SimulationEvent(..))
import Hylograph.Simulation.Emitter (subscribe)

main = do
  -- Run simulation - returns handle AND event emitter
  { handle, events } <- runSimulation
    { engine: Pure  -- or WASM (same config!)
    , setup: setup "physics"
        [ manyBody "charge" # withStrength (static (-30.0))
        , center "center"
        ]
    , nodes: myNodes
    , links: []
    , container: "#my-svg"
    , alphaMin: 0.001
    }

  -- Subscribe to events (framework-agnostic)
  unsubscribe <- subscribe events \event -> case event of
    Tick { alpha } -> log $ "Alpha: " <> show alpha
    Completed -> log "Simulation converged!"
    _ -> pure unit

  -- Get nodes for rendering (use HATS or your own rendering)
  nodes <- handle.getNodes

  -- Update data (GUP semantics, auto-reheat)
  result <- handle.updateData newNodes newLinks
```

## Framework Integration

**Halogen**: Use `toHalogenEmitter` from `Hylograph.Simulation.Halogen`
**React**: Use `subscribe` in a `useEffect` hook with cleanup
**Vanilla**: Just call `subscribe` directly

modules.comments:
HATS Integration for Hylograph Simulation

Provides efficient tick updates for force simulations using HATS templates.

The key insight: simulation nodes change position every tick, but their
structure (radius, color, children) is static. Instead of rebuilding the
full HATS tree at 60fps, we:

1. Initial render: Use full HATS rerender for enter/exit/structural changes
2. Tick updates: Only update transform attribute via fast DOM mutation

## Usage

```purescript
import Hylograph.HATS (forEach)
import Hylograph.HATS.InterpreterTick (rerender)
import Hylograph.Simulation.HATS (tickUpdate)

-- Build your tree with forEach (keyed)
nodesTree = forEach "nodes" Group nodes (\n -> show n.id) nodeTemplate

-- Initial render creates elements with full HATS tree
void $ rerender "#container" nodesTree

-- On each tick, fast-path updates only transforms
-- (nodes array has same elements, just different x/y values)
tickUpdate "#container" currentNodes
```

This gives HATS expressiveness for templates with D3-level performance
for tick updates (~60fps with thousands of nodes).

## Element Requirements

For tickUpdate to work, each node element MUST have:
- `data-id` attribute containing the node's id (as string)
- A `transform` attribute (will be set to `translate(x,y)`)

Example HATS template:
```purescript
nodeTemplate node =
  elem Group
    [ thunkedStr "data-id" (show node.id)  -- Required for tickUpdate
    , thunkedStr "transform" ("translate(" <> show node.x <> "," <> show node.y <> ")")
    ]
    [ elem Circle [...] [] ]
```

declarations.comments:
Fast tick update - only updates transform attribute

Uses direct DOM manipulation to set transform on each node element.
Much faster than rebuilding the HATS tree at 60fps.

Prerequisites:
- Elements must have been created by initial rerender
- Each element must have data-id attribute matching node.id

Call this on simulation tick events when only positions change.
declarations.title: tickUpdate

Like tickUpdate but also updates the radius on child circles.

declarations.comments:
Scene configuration with three-phase lifecycle.

**Phase 1: Initialize** (`initRules`)
Applied before transition starts. Use this to set up starting positions,
e.g., moving tree nodes to the root for a "grow from root" animation.

**Phase 2: Transition** (`layout`)
The interpolation engine smoothly moves nodes from their current positions
to the target positions computed by the layout function.

**Phase 3: Finalize** (`finalRules`)
Applied after transition completes. Use this to set up the stable state,
e.g., unpinning nodes so forces can take over, or setting gridX/gridY.

Example:
```purescript
treeFormScene :: SceneConfig MyNode
treeFormScene =
  { name: "TreeForm"
  , initRules: [ moveToRootRule ]
  , layout: \nodes -> computeTreePositions nodes
  , finalRules: \_ -> [ pinAtTreePositionsRule ]
  , stableMode: Static
  }
```

modules.comments:
One simulation, stepped by its caller, on either engine.

`runSimulation` owns the clock: it ticks on animation frames and tells
you. This is for when you own it: a timeline that can be scrubbed, a
layout computed before anything is drawn, a test. `create` takes the
engine, and everything after that is the same record of functions
whichever engine is behind it, meaning the same thing:

- `step` makes one tick and returns the nodes where it left them;
  `advance` makes several and returns them once;
- `settled` and the three measures say whether it has come to rest;
- `snapshot` and `restore` go back to a moment exactly: the ticks that
  follow a restore are the ticks that followed the snapshot. A snapshot
  carries the tick number, the nodes, the links and the setup, so a
  restore needs nothing else, even after the nodes, links or forces have
  been changed;
- `retarget` gives a Towards force new targets and `reradius` gives a
  Collide, Radial or Contain force new radii, without applying the
  setup again; `reheat` puts alpha back to one; `pin` holds or lets go
  of one node; `relink` puts other links between the same nodes;
- `applySetup` changes the forces and parameters and keeps the nodes
  moving.

THE NODES ARE VALUES. `create` copies the records it is given and never
writes into them. `step`, `nodes` and `restore` return records that are
new after every tick, on both engines. One thing may be written on the
records most recently returned: a pin (`fx`, `fy`, as a drag does),
which the next `step` reads. (The engines underneath differ here, and
this module is where they are made the same: the default engine,
`Hylograph.ForceEngine.Simulation`, adopts the records it is given and
moves them in place, as d3 does; the Rust one,
`Hylograph.ForceEngine.Setup.WASM`, keeps its numbers in the kernel and
makes new records each tick.)

ALPHA is zero once it has fallen below the setup's `alphaMin`, on both
engines (it is the default engine's rule; the kernel alone would go on
cooling), so a force scaled by alpha has then stopped altogether.

The Rust engine needs `initWasm` (or `installKernel`) first, and `free` when done with. The
two engines compute the same rules, the default one in f64 and the Rust
one in f32, so they agree to float width over a tick and drift apart
after that, as any two roundings of a force layout do.
